newsitem.title: CHINA: China Foreign Minister urges pushing U.S. ties.
newsitem.headline: China Foreign Minister urges pushing U.S. ties.

text.p: Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen urged the United States to boost relations on the 25th anniversary of a communique that set the basis for formal ties but warned that Taiwan was the key to steady improvement.
"Under the new circumstances, the need for pushing forward the Sino-U.S. relations is increasing instead of decreasing," state media on Tuesday quoted Qian as telling a seminar in Beijing.

"The potential for strengthening cooperation between the two countries in various fields is expanding instead of shrinking," he told the meeting to mark the 25th anniversary of the Shanghai Communique that formed a basis for the eventual establishment of diplomatic ties between Beijing and Washington in 1979.
However, Qian warned that the issue of Taiwan was crucial to the relationship between the world's top superpower and Asia's fledgling giant.

"The key to the steady development of Sino-U.S. relations is properly handling the question of Taiwan," he said. "This question is related to China's sovereignty, territorial integrity and reunification."

In the Shanghai communique, the United States recognised only one China, but made no comment on its capital or rightful government, hotly contested between Beijing and the Nationalist government in Taipei.
The communique provided the fundamental guiding principle for Sino-U.S. ties, Qian said. Washington established ties with Beijing in 1979 after breaking relations with Taiwan.
Qian made no reference to recent disputes over Taiwan that sent ties plunging to a new lows in 1995 and 1996, signalling a Chinese desire to see a substantical thaw in relations.

Relations between the two Pacific giants plunged last year over several issues, including Taiwan. China pressured Taipei with missile tests and war games ahead of Taiwan's presidential elections last March, prompting Washington to send a naval fleet off the island.

Ties have warmed considerably in recent months, especially since a meeting between Chinese President Jiang Zemin and U.S. President Bill Clinton at the Asia-Pacific Economic Conference forum in Manila last November.
The two sides announced then that they planned an exchange of presidential visits in 1997 and 1998, with Jiang expected to make a state trip to the United States later this year.

The last U.S. president to visit China was George Bush in early 1989. Visits were put on hold after China sent the army to crush student-led demonstrations for more democracy in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in June of that year.
U.S. Vice President Al Gore is expected to pave the way for such an exchange with a visit China later this month during an Asian tour that will include Japan and possibly South Korea.

While the People's Daily newspaper, mouthpiece of China's ruling Communist Party, took a swipe at Washington last week on the 25th anniversary of the communique for failing to honour the terms of its agreements, relations appeared on an upswing.

Barber Conable, chairman of the U.S. National Committee on U.S.-China Relations, warned on Sunday that the Taiwan issue still had the capacity to bring the two countries into "tragic and unnecessary conflict".

However, a visit by new U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright last week appeared to set the seal on improving ties, despite Albright's decision to raise the issue of human rights in China, a thorn in relations.
